paras: The lynching of James Carroll took place on the evening of April 17, 1879, near Point of Rocks, Frederick County, Maryland, when a crowd took Carroll, a young Black man, from two Washington policemen on a Baltimore and Ohio train and hanged him from a tree. Carroll had been arrested in Georgetown that day, accused of an 'outrage' on Mrs. Richard Thomas of Licksville, and was being taken to Frederick for trial. Two Evening Star reporters rode the train and described the seizure, and a coroner's jury found that he had been 'unlawfully hanged' by men unknown.

In a letter dated April 15 to State's Attorney John C. Motter, Richard Thomas wrote that 'a negro named James Carroll' had committed an outrage on his wife the night before while he was away from home. Frederick reports said Carroll had entered the house through a window with a knife, and that more than fifty armed men began searching the country, with the prediction that he would 'certainly be lynched' if caught. Georgetown police first arrested another Black man, Adam Austin, on suspicion, but released him when men from Licksville failed to identify him.

Around noon on April 17, Thomas saw Carroll on the canal tow-path in Georgetown and summoned mounted Officer Volkman, who ran him down with the help of a Mr. Frizzell. According to the Evening Star, Carroll first asserted his innocence, while other reports said he confessed at the station; all agree he agreed to go to Frederick without a requisition.

Officers Volkman and Benjamin F. Harper left Washington with the handcuffed prisoner on the 4:35 p.m. train, accompanied by Thomas. A Frederick County account said a telegram from Thomas's brother, F. C. Thomas, reached Point of Rocks announcing the prisoner's coming, and a mounted messenger spread the word through the neighborhood. Men boarded at Barnesville and Tuscarora to look at the prisoner, and when the train halted at the foot of Sugar Loaf Hill below Point of Rocks station, the car was besieged.

The Star's reporters counted about 75 men, most of the picked fifteen being 'stalwart canal boat men', who held the officers fast while others lifted Carroll out of the car. A noose was put over his head and he was dragged by the neck across the tracks, up an embankment and through a ploughed field toward a clump of woods. The two officers ran after the crowd protesting that 'this must not be done', but were carried back to the train and guarded until it left; Thomas made a dash at Carroll with a knife and was held back.

At a black walnut sapling the rope was thrown over a limb and Carroll was hoisted up, and by the Star's timeline he was dead by 6:45 p.m. Members of the crowd broke twigs from the tree and tore pieces from his clothing as relics before dispersing, some on horseback.

The Evening Star reported that the body hung through the next day in view of railroad passengers until Coroner John Wallace removed it to Frederick on Motter's orders. Frederick's mayor, L. H. Moberly, who said he witnessed the seizure, wrote that the officers 'behaved as officers should' against a crowd no police force could have overcome. On April 21 the coroner's jury, six Democrats and six Republicans, heard witnesses at the Frederick courthouse and, as none knew any of the lynchers, returned a verdict against 'a body of men unknown'. No report of arrests, an indictment or a trial of any lyncher appears in the coverage.

In January 1880 a report of the lynching of George W. Peck at Poolesville recalled that a 'similar scene' had taken place at Point of Rocks the previous April, and in 1882 an Evening Star travel letter still recalled the Tuscarora boarding.

The Washington papers covered the case most fully: the Evening Star ran its reporters' account under the headlines 'LYNCH LAW IN MARYLAND' and 'THE OUTRAGE ON MRS. THOMAS AVENGED', and the National Republican headlined 'SUMMARY VENGEANCE'. Both papers called Carroll 'the Black Ravisher' or 'the Negro Outrager' and treated his guilt as settled, while the Star's editorial called the case 'as nearly a justifiable case of lynching as can well be conceived' but said the lynchers had discredited Maryland's courts.

A Frederick dispatch reprinted in Virginia, West Virginia and Maryland papers called Carroll 'the fiend in human form' and described his death as the vengeance of 'an enraged and outraged community'. The Montgomery County Sentinel and the Shepherdstown Register added that armed men had vowed to attack the Frederick jail if Carroll had reached it. Brief wire versions of the lynching and of the inquest verdict ran in papers from New York and Delaware to Tennessee, Wisconsin, Minnesota and Nevada.

The size and disguise of the crowd varied by account: the Star's reporters saw about 75 men 'without any disguise', the National Republican reported a masked party of fifteen or twenty, the Frederick dispatch nearly three hundred, and the Shepherdstown Register 125 to 150, about 25 of them colored. Accounts of Carroll's words also differ: the Frederick dispatch said he spoke not a word, the Star quoted him crying 'My God, you are killing me', and a Baltimore report said he declared himself guilty but asked for a trial in a court house. The National Republican said the body was cut down after about an hour, while the Star's later report said it hung until the coroner came the next afternoon.

reader.title: Lynching of James Carroll
bases: A crowd took James Carroll, a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman, from two Georgetown policemen on a train near Point of Rocks and hanged him from a tree, and a coroner's jury found him unlawfully hanged by men unknown (A5, A7, A17).

Every account has a body of men, from 15 to nearly 300, seize Carroll from police custody and hang him for an alleged outrage on Mrs. Thomas, and the coroner's jury found he was 'unlawfully hanged' by men unknown (A4, A5, A11, A17).

Eyewitness Star reporters on the train, a National Republican special from Point of Rocks, a Frederick dispatch, a Frederick County narrative and the coroner's verdict agree on the seizure and hanging (A4, A5, A11, A17, A38).

accounts.label: Evening Star reporters on the train
accounts.gist: About 75 men in daylight and without disguise besieged the car; about 15 picked men, mostly canal boatmen, seized Carroll, held the officers, and hanged him from a walnut sapling by 6:45.

accounts.label: National Republican special from Point of Rocks
accounts.gist: Men boarded the train as passengers, a masked party of 15 or 20 entered at a signal, Carroll begged for mercy and was hanged at Snaky Hollow; the lynchers rode away on horses.

accounts.label: Frederick dispatch
accounts.gist: Nearly thirty masked, armed men boarded at Tuscarora; nearly 300 persons, about 100 on horseback, besieged the train at Washington Junction; Carroll said not a word; officers were warned off with pistols.

accounts.label: Frederick County narrative
accounts.gist: A telegram from F. C. Thomas brought 125 to 150 men, about 25 of them colored; twelve or fifteen took Carroll, the rope broke once, and a scramble for mementoes followed.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Carroll was forcibly taken from the train at or near Washington Junction on April 17, 1879, by a body of men unknown to the jury and unlawfully hanged.

framing.detail: The Evening Star ran 'LYNCH LAW IN MARYLAND. THE OUTRAGE ON MRS. THOMAS AVENGED' and called Carroll 'the Black Ravisher', while its editorial said the lynchers discredited Maryland's courts.
The Frederick dispatch called Carroll 'the fiend in human form' who died 'a victim to his brutish passions' and to the vengeance of 'an enraged and outraged community'.
The National Republican headlined 'SUMMARY VENGEANCE. Arrested at Noon and Hanged Before Sundown' while calling Carroll 'the Negro Outrager'.
Short wire items carried the inquest verdict of death 'by persons unknown'.

info: Thursday, April 17, 1879, evening (train reached Sugar Loaf Hill about 6:15-6:32 p.m.; dead by 6:45)

Beside the B. & O. railroad at the foot of Sugar Loaf Hill, about 200 yards below Point of Rocks station at Washington Junction; hanged in a clump of woods (called Snaky Hollow in one account) after being dragged across a ploughed field
James Carroll, a Black man ('negro', 'colored'), aged about 21 to 24, a former canal boatman and farm hand

Accused of an 'outrage' (rape) on Mrs. Richard Thomas (Jennie or Regina Thomas) at Licksville, Frederick County, at night during her husband's absence; also accused of a robbery in another house the same night
A crowd of men from Frederick and Montgomery counties, Md., and Loudoun County, Va.; the Star described most of the picked men as canal boatmen; the inquest named no one
